Nomi: Health Tracker App

The centre of gravity in personal health is moving from treating illness once it arrives to managing the decades before it does, and consumers are now paying out of pocket, at scale, for that shift. This app aims to encourage curiosity rather than anxiety.

2026 · Direction & UI/UX · Figma, Claude Design, Claude Code, HTML/CSS/JS · 1 week · Web (Mobile-First) · Last revised 2026
Hypotheses

Five hypotheses, tested against research

Five assumptions came with the brief. Each was tested against external research rather than intuition, and the findings below reflect what the evidence showed. Hover over each card to see the full finding and its source.

Hypothesis 1

Basic tracking has commoditised

"Heart rate, step count, calories… cheap, ubiquitous, and largely fails to tell users anything actionable."

Most wearables already track things like heart rate, steps, calories, and sleep. These measurements are now cheap and widely available, so simply giving users more numbers does not necessarily help them change their behaviour. The value comes from what the product does with the data, such as explaining it, setting goals, or suggesting what to do next.

Case study
RCT: activity trackers vs. plain pedometers, 16 weeks

Trackers showed no clear advantage over a $10 pedometer for step count or sedentary time in inactive adults, the smart layer added negligible behavioural value on its own.

pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
Hypothesis 2

Deeper markers are more meaningful, contextualised

"VO₂ max, BMR, HRV, muscle fitness, sleep quality… substantially more meaningful, particularly contextualised over time."

Deeper metrics like VO₂ max, HRV, and sleep quality can provide more meaningful insights, especially when viewed over time. However, not all of these measurements are equally reliable. For example, VO₂ max can be useful in certain situations, while sleep staging from a consumer wearable is less reliable. The issue is not that these metrics are useless, but that presenting them with the same level of confidence can make them seem equally accurate.

Case study
Multicentre validation, 11 consumer sleep trackers vs. polysomnography

349,114 epochs, 5 hospitals. Macro F1 scores ranged 0.26 to 0.69 across devices including Oura, Apple Watch and Fitbit: more sophisticated metrics carried wildly inconsistent real-world accuracy.

mhealth.jmir.org/2023/1/e50983
Hypothesis 3

Presentation of complex data is poor

"Numbers, rings and scores are displayed without adequate explanation of what they measure or why they matter."

Many health apps combine several measurements into a single score from 0 to 100. The calculation behind the score is often unclear, so a number like 61 can appear very precise even when users do not know how it was calculated. The problem is therefore not just complicated presentation. The bigger issue is that these scores can make uncertain information feel more accurate and certain than it really is.

Case study
Guardian Angel: LLM-enhanced wearables for LMIC health literacy

Built specifically because users showed "uncertainty in interpreting personal physiological data" from standard wearable displays, a real engineering response to this exact failure, using conversational explanation instead of a raw score.

arxiv.org/pdf/2602.08701
Hypothesis 4

Users need help understanding metrics

"Users need help understanding what each metric means independently, and considerably more help understanding what they mean collectively."

Comprehension and decision-readiness are different things, and the category conflates them. Digital health literacy does predict wearable engagement but understanding a number and knowing what to do about it are separate gaps, and only one of them is being addressed.

Case study
National survey: digital health literacy & wearable use, Germany

Wearable users scored measurably higher on the eHealth Literacy Scale than non-users. Comprehension correlates with adoption, but the study says nothing about whether comprehension alone changes what people then do.

pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov
Hypothesis 5

Education may be the wedge

"Education around these metrics is the weakest part of the current category experience, and may be the wedge."

WHOOP Coach is evidence that education can improve retention, but it is weak evidence that education itself is a durable business wedge. WHOOP already has the data, hardware, brand, and subscription relationship with users. The AI coach adds value on top of that existing ecosystem rather than proving that explanation alone is enough to build and defend a business.

Case study
WHOOP Coach: GPT-4 explainer layered onto existing data

Marketed to "convert curiosity into daily practice." Real, shipped, and credited with improved retention, but bundled inside a $30 per month subscription with elite athlete brand equity built over a decade. Education helped retain existing members, it is not shown to be what wins new ones.

thedatastory.substack.com
Synthesis

What the five verdicts add up to

Read together rather than one at a time, the five verdicts collapse into a single direction, and that direction became the problem statement behind everything else in this walkthrough.

Verdicts
H1
Basic tracking has commoditised
H2
Deeper markers meaningful, but unevenly trustworthy
H3
Presentation asserts false certainty
H4
Comprehension ≠ decision-readiness
H5
Education is not the wedge
What it adds up to
H2 + H3

Looking sophisticated does not always mean the information is reliable.

A complex or less reliable metric presented with the same confidence as a well validated one can create unnecessary worry rather than provide useful insight.

H1 + H4

Basic tracking and better explanations still do not guarantee action.

Understanding a number does not necessarily change what you do. People can own a tracker and understand what HRV means, yet still have no clear reason or direction to act.

H5

Better explanations are not enough

Making health data easier to understand can help people learn, but understanding does not necessarily lead to action. If the goal is to change behaviour, the product needs to do more than explain the data. It needs to help people know what to do next.

Direction this is pointing to

If neither raw data nor better explanation changes behaviour, the category is not failing to inform people. It is rewarding a checking behaviour that informing them does not interrupt, and for someone who already worries about their body, that behaviour is the harm.

Problem Statement

How might we create health tracking that encourages curiosity rather than anxiety, giving people actionable insights while being transparent about what the data can and cannot tell them?

Positioning

Where Our Product sits against the category

The problem statement can be mapped onto two simple questions, then plotted against the category.

  • Prescriptive or descriptive. Does the product tell you what to do, or simply tell you about yourself?
  • Curiosity or fear. Does it bring you back through curiosity, or through fear?

I plotted 10 competitors, and the intended position of this product, on these two axes, based on published research and each product’s own marketing.

Oura's crown icon above 85, Whoop's morning Recovery score, and Apple's closing rings are all extrinsic. Intrinsic return, curiosity about a question you personally committed to, is structurally different and almost unoccupied.

Whitespace

Where the whitespace is

Two spaces in this frame are empty for a business-model reason, not because the idea is bad. Both are where Nomi leans.

Genuinely open

Confidence-transparent health data

No product in the category states uncertainty before a number. Empty because admitting uncertainty is commercially uncomfortable, not because it is a bad business, and it is the direct antidote to the false-precision problem across this category. A composite score with no confidence qualifier is the category's foundational dishonesty.

Genuinely open

Prescriptive and intrinsic, the empty quadrant

The bottom-right of the frame. Products that close the loop with a committed experiment rather than a score, and bring the user back through curiosity rather than streaks. Empty because every incumbent's business model depends on the daily-open metric an experiment loop would cannibalise. That is a business-model wall, not a market verdict.

Why this whitespace stays open

Any competitor can ship a better explainer. Several already have. What none of them can do is restructure the reason a user returns, because their retention models are built on the daily score refresh.

Competitive teardown

Reading the competition honestly

Four positions cover almost the entire category. Each has earned a real strength worth respecting, carries a real weakness worth naming, and has one specific thing that would actually break it.

CompanyReal strengthReal weaknessWhat would break it
Oura Market leadership at 76% ring share, best in class sleep analysis, strongest validation record Only mainstream ring charging a mandatory subscription; zero FDA cleared features on standard models A subscription-free competitor matching app depth. Ultrahuman is explicitly attempting this, and a patent dispute has removed it from US markets, which is itself evidence Oura considers the threat real.

The opportunity space

Two decisions followed directly from where the dots landed.

What I am cutting

The opportunity is not to build another wellness dashboard or performance tracker. Oura and Whoop already serve users who want to monitor and optimise their health. The research points to a different need: helping people understand their health without making it another thing to constantly track or improve. This creates a space for a product built around meaningful insights, clear next steps, and curiosity rather than optimisation.

What is worth keeping

Existing health trackers are good at turning raw sensor data into something people can understand. The opportunity is to take that one step further by turning each insight into one small, practical action, based on something the person is already curious about.

What we measure

Five signals, chosen with purpose

The position only matters if the underlying readings can support it. Five signals were chosen because each helps turn raw data into something meaningful: making changes in stress or sleep easier to notice, and giving some context for why they may have happened.

Signal 01
Overnight HRV

HRV gives us a way to surface changes in how the body may be responding to stress and recovery. For someone who does not actively think about their health, a change in HRV can turn something they only vaguely feel into something they can notice. It looks at the change over time and uses it as a starting point for a more meaningful finding.

Signal 02
Resting heart rate

The most accurately measured metric in the consumer wearable category, the anchor that earns everything else credibility. For the action-stuck user, it is the hero finding: a concrete deviation, the most likely cause in plain language, and the threshold where it would warrant a call to a GP.

Signal 03
Sleep consistency

Duration and timing only, staging excluded. Sleep disruption is the most universal finding across the indifferent group: nearly everyone thinks they sleep well enough, and nearly everyone has a pattern that tells a different story once it is shown against their own history.

Signal 04
Cardio age

HRV and resting heart rate can be difficult to interpret without context. Cardio age gives those signals a more familiar frame of reference. It turns several abstract numbers into one idea that is easier to understand at a glance.

Signal 05
Check-in pattern

Not a physiological signal, a behavioural one: how often, and in what mood, someone opens the app. This is the retention signal for the curiosity habit loop. If checking becomes more frequent because the user is worried, the product has a reason to step back rather than encourage more engagement. That makes checking behaviour part of the product itself.

What we chose not to measure
Rejected
VO2 max

Useful for understanding cardiovascular fitness, but it naturally frames health around performance and improvement. That is not the behaviour the project aims to encourage. This is for someone who wants to understand their body without turning health into another thing to optimise.

Rejected
Sleep staging

REM, deep and light sleep make sleep feel more measurable, but they also introduce more numbers for the user to interpret. For this project, the question is not “How much deep sleep did I get?” It is “Is there a pattern in how I sleep that is worth noticing?” Sleep timing and consistency answer that question with less complexity.

Rejected
Blood oxygen

Can be important in specific clinical contexts, but outside those contexts it is difficult for a generally healthy user to know what to do with a small change. We need readings that can lead to a useful explanation or action. A blood oxygen number on its own often does neither.

Rejected
Strain or training load

Strain and training load are built around performance and recovery, helping users understand how much they have exerted themselves and how to optimise their recovery. This shifts the experience towards performance tracking and optimisation, rather than noticing broader patterns in everyday health. Including it would push the product towards the optimisation mindset it is deliberately trying to avoid.

Rejected
Steps and activity rings

Steps are easy to understand, but that is also part of the problem. They are already familiar, widely available, and easy to track. Adding another step count would give us very little that is distinctive. More importantly, steps do not help answer the type of question we are building around: “Why might I be feeling different?” They tell us what we did, but provide little context for why another signal may have changed.

In summary

Every signal chosen here serves the positioning above: a cause, not just a number, a next step, not a verdict, and a calm explanation before an alarming one. Every reading left out was left out because it pulled toward a grade, a score, or a fear instead, the exact territory this analysis just ruled out. Two questions remain: what device actually captures these signals, and who exactly they are for. The device comes first.

Measurement device

Why a ring, and not a watch

The four signals we chose, overnight HRV, resting heart rate, sleep consistency, and check in patterns, are only useful if the device can measure them reliably. This made the choice of hardware an important part of the product from the start.

DeviceOvernight wearSignal at restBattery lifeScreen distraction
Ring High. Small and comfortable enough that most people keep it on through the night. Strong. The finger artery gives a steady blood flow signal, especially during stillness. Four to seven days. There is no screen drawing power. None. There is no display to check.
Watch or band Low. The bulk and the charging habit mean many nights go unworn. Weaker. The wrist sees more motion artifact and more variation in skin contact. Eighteen to thirty six hours. Frequent charging breaks the overnight habit. High. An always available screen invites streaks and glances.
Chest strap Very low. Almost nobody sleeps in one. Excellent while worn, but essentially never worn overnight. Days, though the point is moot since it is rarely worn to sleep. None, but also unusable for the overnight signals this product needs.

The category already agrees. Oura holds 76% ring share largely on the strength of overnight comfort, so choosing a ring means competing on interpretation and behaviour design, not on re-educating a market about a new form factor.

Trade off accepted

No screen, no room to grow

A ring gives up two things a watch has: a screen for a real time glance, and space for a larger sensor array. Neither cost matters here. All four signals are read afterward, in the app, not glanced at mid workout, and none of them need a sensor a ring cannot carry.

Trade off accepted

Sizing is a real cost

A ring needs a sizing kit and can still be returned when finger size changes throughout the day. A strap or band does not have the same issue. The extra effort is acceptable because sizing only affects the purchase once, not every night the product is worn.

What the ring actually reads
PPG sensor
Overnight HRV & resting heart rate

Green and infrared LEDs shine into the finger artery and a photodiode reads how much light bounces back with every pulse of blood, sampled roughly 250 times a second through the night. That waveform gives both the beat to beat gaps HRV is calculated from and the longest, steadiest stretch used as resting heart rate.

3D accelerometer
Sleep timing & consistency

Motion data marks when the body actually goes still and when it starts moving again, giving a sleep onset and wake time independent of when the wearer thinks they fell asleep. Comparing that timing night to night is what turns one night's data into a consistency pattern.

NTC sensor
Confirms sleep onset

A small dip in skin temperature accompanies the drop in core temperature that comes with falling asleep. Cross checking that dip against the accelerometer's stillness reading is what keeps sleep timing accurate on restless nights.

What this points to

The research points to a gap that is less about measuring more and more about helping people understand what their data means and what to do with it. The opportunity is to make health tracking feel useful and curious, rather than something driven by fear, scores, or optimisation.

Who this is for

  • Two groups stand out: people who avoid health data because it feels irrelevant, and people who want to improve but do not know what to do next.
  • Both groups are poorly served by existing health trackers, which tend to focus on scores, optimisation, or alerts.

Curiosity is a better fit than fear for encouraging people to return without creating anxiety or constant checking. A useful finding needs to lead somewhere, people need a clear next step, not just another number to interpret.

Target audience

Two groups, one pattern

Healthier people actively seek out less health information, not from irresponsibility, but because nothing has made it feel personally relevant. Two groups share that pattern, for different reasons.

Primary

The comfortably indifferent

Broadly healthy, broadly aware they could be doing better. Not in obvious pain, not in crisis. Never opens a health app on their own. Bought a wearable once, abandoned it within six months once the data stopped meaning anything.

The product's job: give one finding that genuinely surprises them, and build from there.
Secondary

The action-stuck

Out of the optimal range on one or more signals, sleep, resting heart rate, HRV, and knows it in a vague way. Told to "improve their lifestyle" by a GP, with no specifics. The category's current answer, a readiness score of 61, gives them a grade with no path.

The product's job: show them what specifically changed, and give them one thing to try this week.

What unites both groups is what they are not motivated by: fear or optimisation. A design built around training, strain, and performance may work well for athletes, but it can push away people who simply want to understand their health without having to optimise it.

Does this differ by gender?
  • The difference is about degree, not a completely different behaviour. Women may be more likely to seek health information and maintain preventive habits, while men are more likely to avoid checking until something prompts them.
  • The common issue is not fear versus curiosity. Both groups can avoid health tracking when it feels like a test they might fail..
  • What differs is how curiosity starts. Some people are drawn in by making the app feel personal, while others are more interested in understanding what their own data means..
  • In all, it should allow people to engage with their health in a way that feels natural to them.
What the pattern points to

Both points to the same conclusion as the research and market analysis: people need a likely explanation instead of a bare number, a clear next step instead of a verdict, and a calm explanation before an alarming one. The hypothesis testing, competitive analysis, and user research provide three different checks, but they all point in the same direction: helping people understand their health is more useful than making them worry about it.

UI Study

How to create a Habit Loop

This creates an opportunity for a product that makes health easier to understand, gives one clear action, and encourages people to check in with curiosity rather than worry.

Cue
Something changed
A single observation the user did not already know.
Curiosity
What caused that?
Ordinary explanations first, ranked by likelihood.
Action
One small experiment
A testable change attached to the insight.
Reward
It moved
The body confirmed what she tried, or ruled it out.
Habit
She checks again
Not from fear, from genuine interest in the answer.

Every answer sharpens the next question, which is what makes the next check-in worth opening. Understanding yourself does not run out the way willpower does, so the habit holds on its own, without needing to be enforced with streaks or guilt.

What makes someone curious, and what makes them anxious

Before any screen was designed, the design questions from the research were mapped on one board: for every way a health app can present a reading, what makes the person on the other side feel curious, and what makes them feel anxious? The bottom half collects the UI patterns other products use to create genuine curiosity.

With that board as the yardstick, 10 visibly different directions were sketched and tested against a single question: does this make someone want to look, or does it make them afraid not to look? Each direction rests on a different, reasonable belief about what brings a person back to a health app.

Explored
62HRV
58BPM
7.2SLEEP
A · Dashboard first

Tested whether seeing every metric at once would build trust through completeness.

Six numbers and charts on the first screen, the standard health app pattern. It put the numbers before their meaning, the exact ordering the hypothesis testing on basic tracking had already ruled out: owning more data does not on its own change what a person does with it. Too data heavy, and it buried the one finding worth noticing under five that were not.

Explored
78
Readiness
score / 100
B · The readiness score

Tested whether a single number would motivate the way it seems to for Oura or Whoop.

One score summarising everything turns health into a leaderboard against yourself, the optimisation mindset both personas actively avoid. It also hides real uncertainty behind a number that looks exact, the same false precision the market analysis later named as the category's most common dishonesty. It encouraged monitoring a score rather than acting on a cause.

Explored
C · Traffic light alerts

Tested whether colour coding every metric would make the state of things legible at a glance.

Legible, but red reads as an emergency even when the truth is only a slightly worse night than usual. The habit loop research is direct about this: fear fades fast and curiosity does not, so a system built on alert colours works against the exact feeling meant to bring someone back tomorrow. It did not support the behaviour Nomi exists to encourage.

Explored
How did I sleep?
Pretty well, 7h 42m…
D · Chat first coach

Tested whether a conversational format would feel more personal than a screen of cards.

Chat puts the burden of curiosity on the person, who has to already know what to ask. The primary persona from the audience research never opens a health app on their own and does not arrive holding a question. A good consultation opens by naming what is worth discussing, it does not wait to be asked. Too much cognitive load for the audience it needed to serve.

Explored
auto advancing in 3… 2… 1…
E · Auto playing stories

Tested whether a timed reveal would carry someone through the recap the way it does on Instagram.

The reveal itself was worth keeping, moving through a recap in short beats works. The countdown was not. Pace pressure on something meant to feel like a calm consultation is a small anxiety mechanism in its own right, and it did not create the kind of motivation to return that curiosity does on its own.

Explored
live BPM ticking
on the home screen
F · Ambient live home

Tested whether a number updating in real time would build the kind of anticipation a live score does.

This came closest to rebuilding the exact problem the research identified. A live number on the screen someone opens most rewards checking without ever asking them to act on what they see, precisely the checking behaviour that does not interrupt anything, and for someone who already worries about their body, that behaviour is the harm itself.

The six explored directions were not bad ideas, but each prioritised completeness, achievement, urgency, or momentum. The final direction instead focuses on understanding the cause, knowing what to do next, and encouraging curiosity rather than repeated checking.

What was kept, and why it works

Four mechanics carried through from concept into the shipped app, and each one passes the same test the six explored directions failed: it should make someone want to look, and it should never make them afraid not to.

Kept
Sophia, your daily summary is ready
Tap to open→
The withheld reveal

The summary hides behind a tap instead of loading in already open. Something worth sixty seconds is named, but not shown, the same instinct behind a wrapped gift rather than an unwrapped one. It creates anticipation with no deadline attached, since nothing here counts down, which is what makes someone want to open it rather than fear what happens if they do not.

Kept
Mo
Tu
We
Th
Fr
Sa
Su
Glowing week pills

Seven circles, one per day, each carrying a state instead of a number: a lime ring means an unopened summary, a flat grey circle means one already seen. An unfinished set is naturally harder to leave alone than a finished one. Nothing here is graded, so closing the ring on a day is curiosity completing itself, not an obligation.

Kept
settlingyour usualplenty of headroom
Zone bands

Every reading lands on a spectrum with encouraging labels at both ends, never a pass or fail colour. A dot sitting closer to one edge invites a look at why, instead of announcing that something is wrong. The same information a traffic light would have flagged in red sits here without ever needing an alarm colour to be understood.

Kept
Terrain chart

Three months drawn as one shape, with any point on it open to a tap. Exploring the past is self directed, a person chooses which day to look into rather than being told to check one. The shape alone shows a trend before a single number does, and nothing on this chart moves on its own the way an ambient live reading would.

Curiosity here is built from anticipation, unfinished loops, and self directed exploration. Anxiety is built from scores, alerts, and countdowns, exactly the mechanics named across the six explored directions above.

Wireframes

Every screen, before any colour

With the map fixed, each of its nodes became a screen. Nomi App: The final UI

Everything above converges here. Nomi (Know me) is the companion app to a sleep ring: each morning it turns the night's readings into one story worth opening, one thing worth trying, and a slowly sharpening picture of what moves your numbers. Built for the two groups who abandoned every tracker before it.

Notice what the loop never asks for: no streak to protect, no score to check, no alert to clear. The only daily commitment is one minute of reading and, if the day allows it, one small experiment. Everything else is optional exploration, which is exactly what keeps it feeling like curiosity instead of homework.

Readings from night one, no verdict yet

  • No comparison yet. There isn't enough history to know what's normal for that person. Instead of a zone or a verdict, each reading shows progress toward building a personal baseline.

Night one · what we heard
7h 18m
A solid first night on record
Sleep duration is the one thing we can read confidently from a single night. Your heart data is in too, 64 bpm resting, 51 ms HRV, but those numbers don't mean anything yet. In two weeks, they'll mean everything.
Baseline · night 1 of 14
TRY
Same wake time tomorrow. Each repeated morning makes night three's reading smarter than night two's.
Keeping someone around with nothing to show yet

A cold start is the highest-risk moment in the product: the app has the least to offer at exactly the point someone is deciding whether it's worth keeping. A few ways to paper over that gap were considered and rejected, since they all worked against rules the rest of Nomi already commits to.

A streak or score from day one

The easiest fix: count something, anything, so the screen always shows a number climbing. Rejected because it manufactures the exact verdict the “no comparison without a baseline” rule exists to prevent.

A checklist scoped to day one

Built: the checklist on screen 7 only asks for what's actually true on night one, wear the ring again tonight, add a tag, nothing that pretends the ring has more to say than it does.

Reminder pushes for missed nights

Nagging notifications bring people back the way an alarm does, through irritation, not curiosity. Rejected for fighting the same habit loop the rest of the product is built around.

A visible, honest countdown

Built: the “night 1 of 14” baseline bar on screen 8 turns the wait itself into something legible. Nothing to compare yet reads as a process with a visible end, not a black box.

Borrowed population averages

Filling the empty zone bar with a stranger's “usual” would give day one something to show, dressed up as a personal reading it isn't. Rejected as a quiet betrayal of the whole premise.

A TRY line on every card, always

Built: even the cards with nothing to grade yet end in an action, keep wearing the ring, tag today anyway, so the app never goes quiet just because it has nothing to score.

A missed night

If a night just doesn't come in

The ring goes uncharged, gets left on the nightstand, or a sync fails, more nights than anyone expects, especially in the first two weeks. The rule: a missed night is never invented, and it never resets the count. The baseline counter only advances on nights that actually have a reading, so a gap just makes the wait one night longer, nothing already collected is lost.

The Today tab

The screen users typically see after several days of readings have been collected. It brings the data together into a simple overview, helping users understand what has changed, why it might have happened, and what is worth paying attention to today.

Today opens on three stacked pieces.

01
Summary
A recap you tap into, revealed one card at a time.
02
Checklist
The same insight, turned into a short list of actions.
03
When you check in
A quiet rhythm chart with no axis, no numbers, just a shape.
Summary

A recap you open, not a report you scan

Why we moved away from one big data card

Nomi's core idea is no numbers thrown at you.

What I did not want

One big card holding every metric at once. Six numbers appearing all together, competing for attention the moment the screen loads, which feels like homework rather than a recap.

What I wanted

Single idea screens that a person taps through, one at a time. This paces the information, so one insight lands before the next appears, and it gives the person control over when to explore each one.

So instead of "here is all your data," the experience becomes "here is one thing worth knowing, would you like to explore it." Health tracking starts to feel less like checking numbers and more like discovering something about oneself.

Borrowed from Spotify Wrapped

Wrapped could publish your year as one page. Instead, it holds every number back until you tap for it, because a number you uncover feels earned in a way a number you are simply shown does not. Nomi borrows the withheld reveal mechanic, not the confetti. Sleep hours, HRV, and the pattern read are unremarkable data points on their own, but releasing them one tap at a time gives each one a beat of weight a table never would.

Try it
This week's summaries tap a day to replay
Ring = unopened · solid = today · dashed = not yet here

Live recreation. Tap the card or any weekday circle. Every day replays the same sample recap so the mechanic is visible. In the real app, each day writes its own.

Under the teaser sits a row of seven circles, one per day of this week, doing quiet double duty as both a calendar and a queue. Each circle carries a state:

  • Lime ring. That day's summary is sitting there unopened.
  • Flat, muted circle. The summary has already been opened, the same visual downgrade a clip gets after it has been watched.
  • Solid fill. Today. There is nothing to open about the day currently being lived.
  • Dashed circle. A day that has not happened yet.
Borrowed from Instagram Stories

Instagram taught a billion people to read a coloured ring as new and a grey ring as done, without a single label. Nomi's week strip uses that exact grammar and repoints it at health data. The ring is not marketing a story, it is marking a summary that has not been opened, so a glance at the row shows not just what happened this week, but what has not been looked at yet.

The Vitals tab

Vitals is for reading the current health stats of the day. The tab holds two things: four readings, and a computation section that turns tags into a personal pattern read.

Readings

Four numbers, read as sentences

Vitals opens on the ring's current readings for the day. Not a dashboard of everything the ring can measure, four numbers only: HRV, resting heart rate, sleep consistency, and cardio age. Each one turns into a short sentence and a position on a bar, never a chart that needs a legend to read.

HRV
How each is measured
ReadingMeasured with
HRV The ring's optical pulse sensor, a light based sensor pressed against the finger artery, reads the tiny gaps between heartbeats through the night. HRV is calculated from how much those gaps vary.
Resting heart rate The same optical pulse sensor, averaged across the lowest, steadiest stretch of the night.
Sleep consistency The ring's motion sensor and skin temperature sensor together, which mark the start and end of sleep each night and compare that timing night to night.
Cardio age No separate sensor. It is computed entirely from the other two readings against typical adult ranges, so it is a calculation, not a measurement.

These four are a deliberate starting set, not the ceiling of what the ring can report. More readings can follow once these four have earned trust.

Timeline

Seeing today next to its neighbors

Vitals originally opened straight onto today's four readings with no way to look sideways. User testing surfaced a gap: a single day's numbers are hard to judge alone, since there is nothing nearby to measure them against. Adding the past several days let a person compare today against a visible run of recent days, rather than trusting one number by itself.

  • Comparison without memory. The last several days sit on screen at once, so nobody needs to recall what Tuesday felt like.
  • Context before conclusion. A single low reading reads differently next to five steady ones than it does alone.
  • One tap, not a new screen. Selecting a different day updates the same four cards in place, so the comparison stays visual rather than becoming a page to page hunt.
  • Builds a habit of checking. Seeing the whole week invites a glance back, not just a glance at today.
Try it
nomi
Vitals
Today, in plain language, and one thing to do about each.

This plays on its own. Tap a day to jump to it, or tap a reading to open it, and it will resume on its own ten seconds after the last tap.

Why a horizontal timeline
  • Familiar shape. A row of date pills borrows the same mental model as a calendar strip or a stories tray, so no explanation is needed.
  • Recency stays reachable. The most relevant days sit at the thumb, on the right, with today anchored at the end.
  • Compact by nature. Seven or more days fit in the height of a single row, leaving the vertical space for the readings themselves.
  • Position doubles as meaning. Distance from the right edge already tells a person how long ago a day was, before they even read the date.
  • Continuity over navigation. The cards update in place rather than opening a new screen, so the days feel like one continuous strip of time rather than seven separate pages.
Cards

Opening a card shows the trend, not just the day

Tapping a card opens it into fourteen days of history, a plain language line comparing today to that trend, an honestly worded line about what the reading cannot tell, and one suggested action.

HRV · recovery
Recovered and ready
64ms
settlingyour usualplenty of headroom
Last fourteen days
HRV has climbed gently over the past two weeks, a slow, quiet trend that usually reflects steadier sleep. Today sits comfortably inside the usual band.
What HRV cannot tell is why. It notices load, such as training, late nights, stress, or a cold brewing, but not which one. Tags fill that gap.
TRY
Green light: a harder session or a demanding day fits well today.

An example of a HRV card, opened.

Why comparing to the past helps
  • One number rarely means much alone. Set against fourteen days, the same reading shows whether it is a blip or a pattern.
  • The body's normal range becomes visible. A person learns their own usual band, not a population average.
  • It quiets the urge to overreact. A single rough morning looks small once it sits beside two weeks of steadier ones.
Curious, not anxious

Nowhere does a card say a number is bad. HRV that sits low reads as Asking for a gentler day, not a warning. A card closes with a line marked TRY, phrased as an invitation rather than an instruction: Favor an easy effort today, like a walk or light session. Recheck tomorrow; one morning is a data point, not a verdict. The goal is curiosity, not alarm: a reading is something to notice and try something about, never something to fear.

A rough day

When every number is low

That claim is easy to make on a good morning. These are the actual card states for a rough one: HRV at its two week low, a heart rate running twelve beats warm, and a sleep rhythm that fell apart. No red appears, nothing is hidden, and each card still ends with something to do.

This is your lowest morning in two weeks, and that's your body doing exactly what it should. A dip this size usually means it's mid-repair: from your run two days ago, a short night, or a bug it's quietly fighting off before you'd ever notice. Dips like this one have always rebounded within a day or two for you.
What one low morning can't tell you: which cause, or whether anything is wrong. It becomes meaningful only if it stays low for several days, and yours never has.

Give your body the easy day it's asking for. Swap the workout for a walk, and let tonight's sleep do the finishing work. Check back tomorrow; the rebound is the interesting part.

Bedtime, this week: drifting later
Bedtime moved around a lot this week. That's it. That's the whole finding. Life clearly had other plans, and your body rolled with them. The good news about body clocks: they forgive quickly. Yours found its way back to 85% within three days the last time this happened, in June.
What this number can't tell you: how well you actually slept. It only measures timing; a great night at an odd hour still counts against it. Your sleep itself was fine this week.

When a dip doesn't let up

Every card above still resolves in a day or two, because that is what a normal dip does. The honesty line only becomes a real signal once a reading breaks that pattern for a person specifically, not against a generic threshold, but against their own history. Here is what the sixth morning in a row looks like, and how the app hands that off without ever raising an alarm.

!HRV, still low: 33 ms against a usual 58, day 6
HRV · recovery
Still not bouncing back
33ms

A single low morning is normal repair. Six in a row without a rebound is not something this app has seen from you before, this is the longest stretch in your history without your usual bounce back.
What this still can't tell you: why. A ring can flag a pattern that has clearly broken from your own baseline, it cannot diagnose what's behind it, that part isn't its job.
TALK

Why a bad morning reads as motivation, not alarm
  • The headline stays kind and stays true. "Asking for a gentler day" describes the same fact a red alert would, but as a request from the body rather than a verdict on it.
  • The number is never softened or hidden. 41 is shown as 41, on the same band as every other day. Honesty is what keeps the kindness credible.
  • The ordinary cause arrives before the frightening one, and your own tags supply it. A tagged social evening explains a warm morning before "something is wrong with my heart" has a chance to form.
  • Each honesty line caps the worry. One low morning is explicitly defined as meaningless on its own, so there is a floor under how far the imagination can fall.
  • TRY converts concern into motion. A walk, water early, one steady wake time. Small enough to actually do, and "the rebound is the interesting part" points curiosity at tomorrow instead of dread at today.

This is the whole thesis of the case study compressed into three screens. The moment most health apps lose their user, the bad morning, is the moment Nomi was designed around.

Tagging

Turning a tag into a personal pattern

Tag Today lets a person mark what the day actually involved: a run, a late meal, a stressful stretch, or anything typed in by hand. Some tags appear on their own, detected by the ring itself and shown with a small dot; the rest are logged by hand.

  • Turns a number into a reason. A dip in HRV means little alone; a dip next to a late meal starts to explain itself.
  • Feeds the person's own data back to them. The pattern read below is built only from this person's tagged mornings, not a population average.
  • Gets sharper with use. Every tagged day adds one more point to compare against, so the read improves the more it is used.
Try it
Tag today
What did today look like? Tags teach the app what moves your numbers, so future summaries get sharper.
Compute
Running a correlation pass across your tagged mornings…
Pattern analysis
A simple pattern compared to your overall baseline, not proof that one causes the other.

Live recreation, running the same correlation math as the app. Select a tag or two and press Compute.

How the read is built, today
1
Gather the tagged days
Every day on record that carries the tag selected, pulled from the full history, not just the recent week.
2
Average the three metrics
HRV, resting heart rate, and sleep consistency, averaged across just those tagged days.
3
Compare to the baseline
The same three metrics, averaged across every day on record, tagged or not. The gap between the two averages is the signal.
4
Score the direction
The gap reads as positive when recovery looks better on tagged days and negative when it looks worse, checked against a short list of which tags are generally expected to help versus cost something.
5
Scale by confidence
Full weight once a tag has been used ten times or more. A tag used once or twice is scaled down, so a couple of tagged mornings cannot outweigh a pattern seen across twenty.
✓
One plain sentence of advice
Worded from the score and the tag's usual reputation, and traceable back to the exact days that produced it.
  • Every result can be explained in one sentence, since the math behind it is just an average and a comparison.
  • It works from day one. A model needs volume to train on; an average needs only one tagged morning to say something, even if a cautious something.
  • Nothing about it is hidden. The advice can be traced back to the exact days that produced it.
What a shipped version would use instead

This is a design concept, so the algorithm is intentionally simple and transparent. A production version would likely use a more advanced model that can learn from many days of data, account for interactions between factors, and adapt to each person’s baseline. For example, a late meal may have a stronger effect after a night of poor sleep, while a recent behaviour may matter more than something that happened months ago. The simple averaging used here is a placeholder for that future model. It keeps the logic easy to understand, so readers can see exactly how each result is produced.

The Health tab

Health is the long view. It holds two things: a continuous chart that compresses three months of mornings into one shape a person can read in seconds, and a selected day card that lets them step back down into any single morning for the full story behind it.

Continuous data

Three months, read as one shape

Health opens on a single chart. Three metrics, HRV, resting heart rate, and sleep consistency, each drawn as a line across a week, a month, or three months, so a person can see their own trend rather than hunt for it across ninety separate mornings.

Try it
Health
Three months of mornings. Tap any point to see that day's story.

Live recreation. Switch the metric or the range, the chart and the at a glance line redraw to match.

How this helps see patterns
  • A line has a shape a single number never does. Ninety mornings laid end to end either climb, dip, or hold level, and a shape is something the eye reads before the mind has to work.
  • Three ranges answer three different questions with the same shape language. A week shows a rough patch, a month shows whether that patch was real, three months shows the season underneath both.
  • Switching the metric keeps the same visual grammar. Learning to read one line teaches a person to read all three.
Absorbing it in seconds

The chart shows the shape. The line underneath it, marked At a glance, names that shape in one sentence, so a person never has to convert a slope into a conclusion by eye. It says the same thing a glance already suspects, just in words, which is what turns a look into an understanding without asking anyone to read an axis.

What gets lost, and why that is fine
  • Every single day's identity fades into the line. That is by design, since across three months no one day is meant to outvote the shape around it.
  • Small day to day noise disappears into the smoothness of the curve. That noise was never the signal, it is exactly what made judging a trend from one morning unreliable in the first place.
  • The reason behind any single dip or climb is not visible here. That is deliberate too. A three month chart's job is to tell a person whether something is worth a closer look, not to explain it, so the explaining is saved for the moment someone actually asks, which is the next section.
The selected day

One tap back down to a single morning

Every point on the chart is a real morning. Tapping one swaps in that day's actual numbers and a short honest explanation for them, turning the trend line from something to admire into something to interrogate.

Try it
stays in sync
replay summary →
What likely happened
TRY

Live recreation. Tap any point on the graph, the card below updates to match. For the last seven days, replay summary reopens that day's full sixty second story, the same format from part one. This demo always plays a generic recap; in the real app, each day writes its own.

Why dropping back down to a day matters
  • A trend explains what happened in general; a single day explains what happened to a person specifically, on a morning they can actually place, such as the trip, or the week they could not sleep.
  • Reconnecting a data point to a memory is what turns a chart from a report into a reflection. The number stops being abstract the moment it is attached to a day someone remembers living.
  • Replay summary goes one step further than a stat readout. It reopens the same story format shown in part one, letting someone relive that morning's sixty seconds rather than just read a caption about it.

Back to the problem statement

3 tabs, built around the 2 questions this case study started with.

Prescriptive over descriptive: the checklist, zone bands, and terrain chart all go beyond showing a number. Each ends with a plain-language explanation and one clear action, so users know what the reading means and what they can try.

Curiosity over fear: the withheld reveals, glowing week pills, encouraging zone labels, and self-guided charts give users a reason to explore without relying on alerts or urgency.

This supports the Nomi direction because Nomi is not trying to compete by measuring more things. It is trying to make existing health data more meaningful and actionable.

User testing

Initial User Feedback

Before this became the version shown above, early builds went in front of a handful of friends, an existing wearable user, and two people who had never opened a health app in their life. Four reactions changed the design outright.

Ultrahuman user
Already fluent in health apps, and the one thing that stood out was the checklist. It read as a short to-do list built from the summary, not another dashboard to maintain, which is what made it stick.
Female tester
Loved being able to set the backdrop to whatever actually made her feel calm. It turned the app into a space she wanted to sit in for a second, not just a screen she checked and closed.
What kind of place calms you?
Mountains
Ocean
Forest
Desert
Male tester
Most drawn to the computation step in Vitals. Digging a real correlation out of his own tagged mornings was something he could not have worked out by eye, and that was the moment the app earned its keep.
Myself, mid-build

Sleep consistency was the one card I kept coming back to. Opened, it first reused the same fourteen-day bar chart every other reading gets, one bar per night, taller meaning more consistent. It technically worked, but a chart built for a value like HRV does not actually explain timing, height alone cannot say whether a night's bedtime was early or late, only how high that night's score happened to be. The redesign swaps that bar chart for one built for what sleep consistency actually is: a row per night showing when bed actually happened, so a late Monday reads as a late Monday instead of just a shorter bar.

Before · opened, same style as resting heart rate
After · opened, redesigned for sleep consistency

What's next

This whole project, research, positioning, personas, UI, and this walkthrough, was built solo in one week. That constraint shaped what got explored deeply and what got left as a note for later. A few honest ones below.

Marketing strategy

The hardware pattern in this category leans two ways: a one-time payment bundled with the ring, or a subscription that keeps unlocking software as the ring keeps shipping data. Nomi could plausibly sell the ring as a one-time purchase covering the core loop, readings, the checklist, zone bands, and the terrain chart, and hold back a smaller set of genuinely deeper features behind an optional membership: the tag-correlation engine test users responded to most strongly, a full history past three months, and additional backdrop themes beyond the starting set. That mirrors what the category already does, Oura sells a $300+ ring that still asks for a monthly fee to unlock the full app, and Whoop skips the hardware fee entirely in favour of a pure subscription. Testing here pointed the same direction: the free core has to feel complete enough to be worth keeping on its own, and the paid layer should be the part someone specifically asks “wait, can it also do X?” about, never a paywall on the basics.

The screen below reuses components already shipped in the app, no separate marketing assets, the checklist card, zone-band language, and accent colour doing the same job in a paywall that they do on Today and Vitals.

Areas of improvement

The features that shipped were the ones the five hypotheses pointed to directly. A few adjacent ideas came up during research and testing but never made the cut for week one, worth naming here as what to explore next rather than as gaps in the current build.

  • Passive sync from Apple Health or Google Fit. The tag-correlation engine currently only sees what a person types into Tag Today. Reading in caffeine, workouts, or screen time already logged elsewhere would give it context the ring alone can't capture, without adding a single new question to onboarding.
  • Voice check-in. Typing a tag before getting out of bed is friction at exactly the moment the app most wants a response. A ten-second voice note, transcribed into the same tag format Tag Today already uses, would fit that half-asleep context better than a keyboard does.
  • An opt-in partner view. A couple of testers wanted a low-stakes way to loop in a partner, not the raw numbers, only the day's checklist item, so someone else can nudge them without turning health data into something shared by default.
What I'd revisit with more time

Stepping back from the whole thing rather than any one screen, a few bigger questions stood out, the kind a senior reviewer would flag in a critique, not bugs so much as places I made a call in a week that deserves more thought than a week allows.

  • Where curiosity risks tipping into compulsion. The daily reveal is inspired by patterns like unread dots and "someone liked you," the exact kind of hook the whole positioning argues against. I'd want a clearer line for how far that pattern is allowed to go before it stops being genuine curiosity and starts being a compulsion loop.
  • What Nomi says to someone whose “usual” is never good. Almost every card is written against a person's own baseline eventually rebounding. That works for a healthy person's rough week, but someone with a chronic condition may never have a baseline worth returning to, their normal already looks like the six-day escalation case. I'd want to design specifically for that person, not assume everyone bounces back.
  • Whether two personas capture enough real variation. The two personas are useful shorthand, but they say nothing about age, pregnancy, menopause, shift work, or disability, all of which change what a normal HRV or sleep pattern even looks like. And because the usability testing plan above recruits along those same two personas, that same gap would carry straight into the next round of research if I didn't fix it first.
Depth and research limitations

The five hypotheses were checked against published research, not built from primary research of my own, and the ten competitors on the positioning map were plotted from public marketing and reporting, not hands-on trials of each app. Given more time, I would want to validate the correlation engine's outputs against something closer to ground truth, and spend real time inside Oura, Whoop, and Ultrahuman rather than reading about them secondhand.

Conducting more usability testing

The reactions shown earlier are real, but they are four people, three friends and myself, not a study. What is missing is a proper round, and the design of that round matters: a single sitting only tests whether the interface is legible, not whether curiosity actually outlasts fear once the novelty of a new app wears off. Here is how I would run it.

01
Screen and recruit
10–12 participants split across the two personas research surfaced: proactive information-seekers and avoidant checkers, recruited outside my existing network this time.
02
Moderated think-aloud
A 60-minute remote session per participant: live onboarding, the first night's reading, one Tag Today entry, narrated as they go so hesitation is caught as it happens.
03
Unmoderated diary study
14 nights, matching the app's real baseline window. A two-question daily prompt after each open, unwatched, since a moderator in the room changes the exact behaviour this phase needs to observe.
04
Closing interview
A short call after night 14 to ask directly whether the app still felt worth opening once it stopped being new, and why.
05
Synthesis
Use usability scores from phase two as the baseline, then measure what really matters: whether people feel curious or obligated to use the app, and whether they actually come back between days 8 and 14. Compare these results to see which experience creates stronger long term engagement.

The two phases answer different questions:

Phase two asks, “Can people use the app?”
Phase three asks, “Do people keep coming back because they are genuinely curious, even after the app is no longer new?”

Stopping at phase two would only tell us whether the app is usable. It would not tell us whether the experience actually creates lasting curiosity and engagement.

What I'd test too

Test different ways of creating curiosity, rather than choosing one approach based mainly on online research.

Possible user experiments:

  • First impression test. Show different versions and ask users what they would tap first, and why.
  • Reveal test. Compare a withheld reveal, a live reveal, and an immediate insight to see which creates more interest.
  • Action test. Give users the same insight with different suggested actions and see which feels most useful or motivating.
  • Return test. Ask users to use each version over several days and track which experience they voluntarily return to.
  • Understanding test. After seeing an insight, ask users to explain what they think happened and what they would do next.

Measure both: which version gets people interested initially, and which one gives them a reason to come back.

Goal: use real user behaviour and feedback to determine which interaction creates lasting curiosity, rather than relying only on research or design intuition.

Process

How I use AI in my design process

Research and synthesis

I use AI to organise research, identify patterns across findings, challenge assumptions, and help turn large amounts of information into clearer design opportunities.

Exploration and ideation

AI helps me quickly explore different directions, UI patterns, information structures, and interaction ideas before committing to a single solution. This allows me to test more possibilities within a shorter timeframe.

Prototyping and iteration

I use tools such as Claude Code to turn design ideas into functional prototypes and live interfaces. This allows me to move beyond static screens and quickly test how an experience actually feels and behaves.

Content and UX writing

AI helps refine UX copy, simplify complex information, and explore different ways of communicating an insight. I still make the final decisions based on the intended user experience and product tone.

Design critique

I also use AI as a second perspective during the design process. I can challenge a design direction, ask it to identify inconsistencies, or test whether the reasoning behind a design decision is strong enough.

Closing thoughts

Health data doesn't need to be bigger. It needs to be kinder.

Every screen in this case study, the checklist, the zone bands, the withheld reveal, the six-day escalation, was one answer to the same question: what does it look like to tell someone the truth about their body without making them afraid of it? A week wasn't enough to prove that answer right, only enough to build it carefully and be honest about where it still needs work.

What I'd want a reader to take from this isn't the ring, or the checklist, or any one screen. It's the discipline underneath all of them: every number gets a plain-language reason before it gets a verdict, every honesty line admits what the data can't say, and every hard moment still ends with something small and doable. That discipline is the actual product. Nomi is just where I first tried to build it end to end.
